title: Lipids: The Building Blocks That Refuse to Polymerize

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: What single property defines the lipids as a class of biomolecule?
cards.back: Solubility in organic solvent: a definition by behavior, not by a shared structure.
cards.quote: The only property that unites them is solubility in organic solvent, a definition by behavior rather than by structure.
cards.section: Lipids break the rules

cards.front: Proteins, DNA and polysaccharides are polymers. Why are lipids not, and what are they built from instead?
cards.back: They are not chains of repeating monomers. They are assembled combinatorially from modular parts: fatty acids, glycerol, sphingosine and sterols, mixed and matched.
cards.quote: They are assembled combinatorially from a small kit of modular parts: fatty acids, glycerol, sphingosine and sterols, mixed and matched.
cards.section: Lipids break the rules

cards.front: A fatty acid's carboxyl group has a pKa of about 4.8. In what form is it mostly found at pH 7.4, and how is that form named?
cards.back: Almost entirely deprotonated, as the carboxylate ion. Biochemists name the ion: palmitate for palmitic acid, oleate for oleic acid.
cards.quote: That acid group has a pKa of about 4.8, so at pH 7.4 it has almost entirely lost its proton
cards.section: Fatty acids: why one bend melts a fat

cards.front: Decode the fatty acid shorthand 18:1 cis-Δ9.
cards.back: 18 carbons, one double bond, starting at carbon 9 counted from the carboxyl (acid) end, in cis geometry.
cards.quote: Carbons are counted from the acid end, so Δ9 means the double bond starts at carbon 9.
cards.section: Fatty acids: why one bend melts a fat

cards.front: How does the chain geometry at a cis double bond differ from that at a trans double bond in a fatty acid?
cards.back: Cis: the two parts of the chain leave from the same side, so the chain bends by about 30°. Trans: they leave from opposite sides, and the chain stays nearly straight.
cards.quote: In a cis double bond, the two parts of the chain leave from the same side, so the chain bends by about 30°.
cards.section: Fatty acids: why one bend melts a fat

cards.front: Why do longer saturated fatty acids (laurate 12:0 at 44 °C up to stearate 18:0 at 70 °C) melt at higher temperatures?
cards.back: A longer straight chain has more length in van der Waals contact with its neighbors, so more heat is needed to shake it free of the ordered packing.
cards.quote: A longer pencil has more length in contact, so it takes more heat to shake it free.
cards.section: Fatty acids: why one bend melts a fat

cards.front: Oleate (18:1 cis-Δ9) differs from stearate (18:0, melts at 70 °C) only by one cis double bond at carbon 9. Predict whether oleate melts a little or a lot lower, and why.
cards.back: A lot lower: near 13 °C, about 57 degrees below stearate, so it is liquid at room temperature.
cards.why: The kink weakens no bond (a double bond is stronger than a single one); it changes shape, so far less chain length is in contact with neighbors.
cards.quote: Far below: oleate melts near 13 °C, about 57 degrees lower than stearate, so it is liquid at room temperature.
cards.section: Fatty acids: why one bend melts a fat

cards.front: State the packing rule that links a lipid tail's structure to its melting point.
cards.back: Lined-up tails stick by van der Waals contact. Anything that adds contact (a longer, straight tail) raises the melting point; anything that removes it (a cis kink, the first most of all) lowers it.
cards.quote: Anything that adds contact (a longer, straight tail) raises the melting point, and anything that removes it (a cis kink, the first kink most of all) lowers it.
cards.section: Fatty acids: why one bend melts a fat

cards.front: What can the lipid packing rule (more tail contact, higher melting point) not do?
cards.back: It ranks two lipids that differ in one dial, but it gives no exact temperatures and cannot settle a trade-off between a longer chain and an extra kink.
cards.quote: It does not give exact temperatures, and it cannot settle a trade-off between a longer chain and an extra kink.
cards.section: Fatty acids: why one bend melts a fat

cards.front: In the 18-carbon series, stearate (18:0) melts at 70 °C, oleate (18:1) near 13 °C and linoleate (18:2) near −5 °C. How much does each added cis bond lower the melting point, and what does the comparison show?
cards.back: First bond: 70 − 13 = 57 degrees. Second bond: 13 − (−5) = 18 degrees. The first kink does most of the work; once packing is broken, each further bend removes less (in the 18-carbon series, at least up to three double bonds).
cards.quote: Add a second cis bond (linoleate, 18:2) and the melting point falls only about 18 degrees more, to about −5 °C.
cards.section: Fatty acids: why one bend melts a fat

cards.front: Elaidate is the trans twin of oleate: a trans double bond at carbon 9 leaves the chain nearly straight. Stearate melts at 70 °C and oleate near 13 °C. Where should elaidate melt?
cards.back: Between them, a little nearer stearate: about 45 °C, close to halfway.
cards.why: A nearly straight chain packs much better than a bent cis chain, but well short of a saturated chain.
cards.quote: Between them, a little nearer stearate: about 45 °C, close to halfway.
cards.section: Fatty acids: why one bend melts a fat

cards.front: Why does partial hydrogenation turn a liquid vegetable oil into a spreadable fat?
cards.back: It turns some cis bonds trans and saturates others. Straighter chains pack better, so the melting point rises.
cards.quote: This is why partly hydrogenating a vegetable oil, which turns some cis bonds trans and saturates others, makes a liquid oil spreadable.
cards.section: Fatty acids: why one bend melts a fat

cards.front: Stored fat is a {{c1::triacylglycerol}}: three fatty acids joined by ester bonds to a glycerol backbone.
cards.quote: Stored fat is a triacylglycerol: three fatty acids joined by ester bonds to a glycerol backbone.
cards.section: Triacylglycerols: three tails on glycerol

cards.front: Predict the state at room temperature of tripalmitin (three palmitates on glycerol), of triolein (three oleates), and of a natural fat that mixes saturated and unsaturated chains.
cards.back: Tripalmitin: a high-melting solid. Triolein: liquid. The mixed fat: an intermediate melting point.
cards.why: The packing rule carries over; a fat's melting behavior is set mostly by which fatty acids it carries.
cards.quote: Tripalmitin, three saturated palmitates on one glycerol, is a high-melting solid.
cards.section: Triacylglycerols: three tails on glycerol

cards.front: Lard is solid on the counter and olive oil pours. Using their fatty acid content and the packing rule, explain the difference.
cards.back: Lard carries more straight saturated chains (palmitate, stearate) that pack tightly and melt high. Olive oil is mostly oleate, whose cis kink cuts contact and drops the melting point below room temperature.
cards.why: A triacylglycerol's melting behavior is set mostly by which fatty acids it carries, so the free fatty acid ranking carries over to whole fats.
cards.quote: Lard carries more straight, saturated chains such as palmitate and stearate.

cards.front: What drives phospholipids to assemble into a bilayer in water, with no ATP and no proteins?
cards.back: The hydrophobic effect. Exposed tails force water into ordered cages; tucking the tails together frees that water, and the gain in water's entropy drives assembly.
cards.quote: Tucking the tails together frees that water to tumble again, and that gain in water's entropy, its disorder, drives assembly.
cards.section: Why lipids make bilayers (a separate rule)

cards.front: Describe a simple lipid bilayer below and above its transition temperature, Tm.
cards.back: Below Tm: tails straight and packed in order, a stiff gel. Above Tm: tails flex and slide, a fluid in which proteins can move and work. (Real membranes are mixtures, with a higher, broader transition.)
cards.quote: Below Tm the tails are straight and packed in order, and the membrane is a stiff gel.
cards.section: Bilayers melt too: gel and fluid

cards.front: Phosphatidylcholine Tm values: DPPC (16:0/16:0) 41 °C, POPC (16:0/18:1 cis) −2 °C, DOPC (18:1 cis/18:1 cis) −17 °C. How much does each oleate swap lower Tm, and what does this show?
cards.back: First swap: 41 − (−2) = 43 degrees. Second swap: −2 − (−17) = 15 degrees. As in free fatty acids, the first kink does most of the work.
cards.quote: Swapping one saturated tail of DPPC for oleate drops Tm by 43 degrees.
cards.section: Bilayers melt too: gel and fluid

cards.front: E. coli growing at a warm temperature is moved to the cold, and its membrane starts to stiffen as it nears its Tm. What should it change about its membrane lipids, and why?
cards.back: Make more unsaturated fatty acids. More cis kinks mean less contact, so Tm falls below the new, colder temperature and the membrane stays fluid.
cards.why: Tuning composition to hold viscosity constant as the environment changes is homeoviscous adaptation.
cards.quote: Make more unsaturated fatty acids, as E. coli does.
cards.section: Bilayers melt too: gel and fluid

cards.front: A bacterial mutant cannot make unsaturated fatty acids. It is shifted from a warm to a cold temperature. Predict the state of its membrane and the effect on its membrane proteins.
cards.back: Without new unsaturated fatty acids it loses its main means of lowering Tm, so if the cold brings the membrane near or below Tm it tends to stiffen toward a gel, where proteins move less freely.
cards.why: Rests on two rules: unsaturation is the cell's main dial for Tm (homeoviscous adaptation), and only the fluid state lets membrane proteins move and work.
cards.quote: Unsaturation is the main dial: the packing rule, run by the cell.
cards.section: Bilayers melt too: gel and fluid

cards.front: Describe cholesterol's structure and how it sits in a membrane.
cards.back: A rigid tetracyclic steroid about as long as a 16-carbon fatty acid, spanning one leaflet: hydroxyl at the head-group interface, rings against neighboring chains, tail in the core.
cards.quote: Cholesterol is a rigid tetracyclic steroid about as long as a 16-carbon fatty acid, spanning a single leaflet.
cards.section: Cholesterol, the buffer

cards.front: Adding cholesterol to a fluid membrane (above Tm) makes it more ordered. What does adding cholesterol do to a membrane below Tm, in the gel state, and why?
cards.back: It makes the gel more fluid. Its bulky rings sit between tails that would otherwise line up and crystallize.
cards.why: In a fluid membrane the same flat, rigid rings lie against neighboring tails and stop them flexing.
cards.quote: In a gel, the same bulky rings sit between tails that would otherwise line up and crystallize.
cards.section: Cholesterol, the buffer

cards.front: Why is cholesterol called a membrane thermostat rather than a heater or an air conditioner?
cards.back: It acts in both directions: it orders fluid membranes and fluidizes gels. Rather than just shifting the melting point, it broadens the whole transition.
cards.quote: Cholesterol is a thermostat, not a heater or an air conditioner: rather than just shifting the melting point, it broadens the whole transition.
cards.section: Cholesterol, the buffer

cards.front: Two DPPC bilayers (Tm 41 °C), one pure and one containing cholesterol, are each heated from 20 °C to 60 °C while fluidity is measured. How will the two gel-to-fluid transitions compare?
cards.back: Pure DPPC: a sharp step near 41 °C. With cholesterol: a gentle slope, more fluid than pure DPPC below the transition and more ordered above it.
cards.why: Combines the bilayer melting rule (a pure lipid has a sharp Tm) with cholesterol's two-way buffering, which broadens the transition.
cards.quote: then add cholesterol and watch the sharp gel-to-fluid step flatten into a gentle slope.
cards.section: Cholesterol, the buffer

cards.front: Why does fat carry about 9 kcal/g while carbohydrate carries about 4 kcal/g?
cards.back: Fat's carbon is more reduced. Its carbons are almost all CH₂, while each glucose carbon already carries an oxygen, so glucose is partly burned before you start.
cards.quote: Its carbons are almost all CH₂, while each carbon of glucose already carries an oxygen, so glucose is partly burned before you start.
cards.section: The other job: fuel (a separate rule)

cards.front: Besides being more reduced, what second property makes fat a far more compact energy store than glycogen?
cards.back: Fat is stored nearly anhydrous, while glycogen is stored hydrated, binding about 2 g of water per gram or more (estimates vary).
cards.quote: Second, fat is stored nearly anhydrous (without water), while glycogen is stored hydrated, binding about 2 grams of water per gram or more (estimates vary).
cards.section: The other job: fuel (a separate rule)

cards.front: A 70 kg person stores about 135,000 kcal as fat. Taking fat at 9 kcal/g and glycogen at 4 kcal/g with 2 g of water per gram, what would that energy weigh as fat and as hydrated glycogen?
cards.back: Fat: 135,000 ÷ 9 ≈ 15,000 g, about 15 kg. Wet glycogen: 4 kcal per 3 g ≈ 1.33 kcal/g, so 135,000 ÷ 1.33 ≈ 100,000 g, about 100 kg. About 85 kg extra.
cards.quote: As glycogen: take 2 g of water with each gram, so 3 g of wet store holds 4 kcal, about 1.33 kcal per wet gram.
cards.section: The other job: fuel (a separate rule)

cards.front: Fat holds about 9 kcal/g; glycogen holds 4 kcal/g of dry weight. If glycogen bound 3 g of water per gram instead of 2, how many times more energy per wet gram would fat hold?
cards.back: Wet glycogen: 4 kcal per 4 g = 1 kcal/g. Fat: 9 ÷ 1 = 9-fold, up from about 6.75-fold with 2 g of water.
cards.why: Rests on the stated rule that fat's advantage per wet gram grows the more water glycogen holds.
cards.quote: Per wet gram, fat holds 9 ÷ 1.33 ≈ 6.75 times as much energy, about sevenfold, and more if glycogen holds more water.
cards.section: The other job: fuel (a separate rule)

cards.front: Lipids do three things covered by different rules: melt and set membrane fluidity, assemble into bilayers, and store fuel. Which rule explains each?
cards.back: Melting and fluidity: the packing rule (tail contact). Bilayer assembly: the hydrophobic effect (water's entropy). Fuel: fat's reduced carbon and dry storage. Fuel has nothing to do with packing.
cards.quote: Fat's value as fuel has nothing to do with packing.
cards.section: The other job: fuel (a separate rule)

cards.front: What do flippases, floppases and scramblases each do to membrane lipids?
cards.back: Flippases: ATP-driven, move particular lipids to the inner leaflet. Floppases: ATP-driven, move lipids outward. Scramblases: when switched on, let lipids cross both ways, erasing asymmetry.
cards.quote: flippases are ATP-driven pumps that move particular lipids to the inner leaflet, and floppases move lipids outward, also using ATP.
cards.section: Membrane identity: head groups and leaflets

cards.front: Give the net charge and usual leaflet of phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylserine (PS) in the plasma membrane.
cards.back: PC: no net charge, outer leaflet (with sphingomyelin). PE: mostly inner. PS: negative, held on the inner leaflet, where positively charged cytoplasmic proteins meet it.
cards.quote: Phosphatidylserine (PS) is negative and is held on the inner leaflet, where positively charged cytoplasmic proteins meet it.
cards.section: Membrane identity: head groups and leaflets

cards.front: How does phosphatidylinositol (PI) serve as a signaling lipid?
cards.back: Its phosphorylated form, PIP₂, is cleaved by phospholipase C into two messengers: DAG (diacylglycerol) and IP₃ (inositol trisphosphate).
cards.quote: its phosphorylated form, PIP₂ (phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate), is cleaved by phospholipase C into two messengers, DAG (diacylglycerol) and IP₃ (inositol trisphosphate).
cards.section: Membrane identity: head groups and leaflets

cards.front: What is distinctive about cardiolipin's structure and location?
cards.back: It has two phosphates and four tails, and it lives almost only in the mitochondrion.
cards.quote: Cardiolipin, with two phosphates and four tails, lives almost only in the mitochondrion.
cards.section: Membrane identity: head groups and leaflets

cards.front: A cell begins apoptosis: its flippases shut off and its scramblases switch on. What happens to phosphatidylserine (PS), and what follows?
cards.back: PS reaches the outer surface. A macrophage reads externalized PS as an "eat me" signal and engulfs the dying cell before it bursts and inflames the tissue.
cards.quote: a macrophage reads externalized PS as an "eat me" signal, engulfing the dying cell before it bursts and inflames the tissue.
cards.section: Membrane identity: head groups and leaflets

cards.front: A cell line lacks scramblase activity. It is triggered into apoptosis and its flippases shut off. Predict its PS exposure and its clearance by macrophages compared with a normal apoptotic cell.
cards.back: PS is not expected to reach the outer surface, so the "eat me" signal should be missing or weak; clearance would then be expected to be impaired.
cards.why: Rests on the stated rule that PS reaches the outer surface when flippases shut off and scramblases switch on; without scramblase activity the outward route is missing.
cards.quote: Scramblases, when switched on, let lipids cross both ways and erase the difference.
cards.section: Membrane identity: head groups and leaflets

cards.front: Which bond tells a glycerophospholipid from a sphingolipid?
cards.back: Glycerophospholipids attach their tails to glycerol, usually by ester bonds. Sphingolipids use an 18-carbon sphingosine backbone with one amide bond. Ester versus amide.
cards.quote: Sphingolipids use an 18-carbon sphingosine backbone with one amide bond.
cards.section: Membrane identity: head groups and leaflets

cards.front: Why are glycolipids called the cell's name tag?
cards.back: Their sugars face outward only, advertising the cell's identity to the immune system.
cards.quote: Their sugars face outward only, advertising the cell's identity to the immune system.
cards.section: Membrane identity: head groups and leaflets

cards.front: Name the three ways proteins associate with membranes.
cards.back: Integral (in the hydrophobic core), peripheral (on the surface by ionic and hydrogen bonds), and lipid-anchored (tethered by a covalently attached lipid such as palmitate, farnesyl or a GPI anchor).
cards.quote: Proteins associate with membranes in three ways.
cards.section: Proteins at the membrane

cards.front: Membrane protein X is released by a high-salt wash. Protein Y comes off only with detergent. Classify each and explain the result.
cards.back: X is peripheral: salt disrupts the ionic and hydrogen bonds holding it to the surface. Y is integral or lipid-anchored: its hydrophobic segment or anchor is buried in the core.
cards.quote: A salt or pH change frees a peripheral protein.
cards.section: Proteins at the membrane

cards.front: A protein needs detergent to leave the membrane, yet a specific phospholipase also releases it. What kind of membrane attachment does this suggest?
cards.back: A GPI anchor. Detergent frees most lipid-anchored proteins through the buried anchor, and a specific phospholipase can cut a GPI-anchored protein loose.
cards.quote: a GPI-anchored protein can also be cut loose by a specific phospholipase.
cards.section: Proteins at the membrane

cards.front: How does a transmembrane alpha-helix cope with the lipid core, and about how many hydrophobic residues does it need?
cards.back: The core offers no hydrogen-bond partners for backbone amides, so the helix satisfies its own backbone internally. About 20 hydrophobic residues cross the roughly 30-angstrom core.
cards.why: A beta-barrel solves the same problem by hydrogen-bonding strand to neighboring strand.
cards.quote: An alpha-helix solves this by satisfying its own backbone internally, taking about 20 hydrophobic residues to cross the roughly 30-angstrom core
cards.section: Proteins at the membrane

cards.front: Why are linoleate (omega-6) and α-linolenate (omega-3) essential in the human diet?
cards.back: Human desaturases cannot place a double bond between carbon 10 and the methyl end; we lack Δ12 and Δ15 desaturases, where omega-6 and omega-3 bonds sit.
cards.quote: In an 18-carbon chain, an omega-3 double bond sits at Δ15 and an omega-6 at Δ12, both out of reach.
cards.section: Omega numbering and essential fatty acids

cards.front: An NSAID blocks cyclooxygenase. Predict its effects on pain and fever, and on the stomach lining, and explain both.
cards.back: Less pain, fever and inflammation, but stomach irritation. Cyclooxygenase turns arachidonate into prostaglandins, and the same prostaglandins (made by COX-1) protect the gastric lining.
cards.quote: NSAIDs block that enzyme, which is also why they irritate the stomach: the same prostaglandins (made by COX-1) protect the gastric lining.
cards.section: Prostaglandins and NSAIDs

cards.front: Palmitate (16 carbons) yields about 106 ATP; glucose (6 carbons) yields about 30–32 ATP. Compute ATP per carbon for each and explain the gap.
cards.back: Palmitate: 106 ÷ 16 ≈ 6.6 ATP per carbon. Glucose: 30–32 ÷ 6 ≈ 5.0–5.3, about 5.2. Glucose's carbons already carry oxygen, so they are less reduced.
cards.quote: Per carbon it is about 6.6 ATP against about 5.2, and the gap is the oxygen glucose's carbons already carry.
cards.section: Fuel per molecule and per carbon
